article_title: R.I. legislators of color back seven immigration bills to counter ICE actions
article_content:
PROVIDENCE — With Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents seizing people outside courthouses and schools, Rhode Island legislators of color are making a package of immigration bills their top priority for the 2026 legislative session.
The Rhode Island Black, Latino, Indigenous, Asian-American and Pacific Islander Caucus is backing seven bills that would, among other things, prohibit civil arrests at state courthouses without a judicial warrant, limit the use of face masks by ICE agents; and allow Rhode Island residents to sue federal officials in state courts for violating their constitutional rights.
“People are living in real fear,” state Senator Tiara T. Mack, a Providence Democrat and the caucus cochair, said during a news conference. “People are not going to work. People are keeping their children from school. We’ve heard horror stories.”
She noted that in November, ICE agents wrongfully detained a high school student who was a state Superior Court intern outside a Providence courthouse and only released him after a judge intervened. She said she also received a text message last week saying someone was detained near another state courthouse in Providence after supporting a family member in court.
“This immigration package is bigger than Rhode Island,” said Mack, who is cochairing the Federal Response Coalition of the State Futures national nonprofit group. “These are seven bills that are part of 225 bills and counting moving across 35 states on the rule of law and immigration.”
Mack said she has introduced a bill that would allow expanded use of virtual or remote court hearings for “Rhode Islanders who are afraid of traveling to their hearings because they know that ICE waits outside of courtrooms daily.” Representative Grace Diaz, a Providence Democrat, will sponsor the House version of that bill.
Also, Senator Meghan E. Kallman, a Pawtucket Democrat, said she and Representative Jose F. Batista, a Providence Democrat, have introduced a bill that would prohibit civil arrests at Rhode Island courthouses without a valid judicial warrant.
That legislation “is an antidote to address the growing tide of immigration enforcement taking place at or near courthouses in the state,” Kallman said. “Justice cannot work if people are afraid to walk through the door.”
On any given morning in Providence, hundreds of people enter state courthouses, including survivors of domestic violence, witnesses, and defendants, she said.
“But increasingly, many of them are afraid,” Kallman said. “They are afraid that masked federal agents are going to pick them up and disappear them.”
The bill does not prohibit federal immigration enforcement, she said. “It simply requires that if someone is going to be arrested outside a courthouse, the decision must first be reviewed and approved by a judge,” she said.
Representative Jenni A. Furtado, an East Providence Democrat, and Mack have introduced legislation that would prohibit state and local law enforcement agencies from entering into 287(g) agreements with ICE — pacts that green-light local law enforcement to act as immigration agents.
“Perhaps this goes without saying, but right now federal immigration policy is cruel, reckless, lawless, and chaotic,” Furtado said. “Enforcing it in our communities would be completely incompatible with community safety and a trusting relationship between law enforcement and Rhode Island residents.”
Nine states, including Connecticut, have laws prohibiting 287(g) agreements, Furtado said, and such legislation has been introduced in Massachusetts.
“It is time we join them and make sure that our local police departments keep doing the hard work to uphold violence laws and protect its residents,” Furtado said. “Local police are not tools for the whims of the White House, and this bill ensures that they stay that way.”
Senate Majority Leader Frank A. Ciccone III, a Providence Democrat, and Representative Brandon C. Potter, a Cranston Democrat, have introduced a bill that would create a state-level civil cause of action allowing people to sue when federal officials, acting under federal authority, violate rights guaranteed under the US Constitution.
“Across the country and here at home, we have seen consequences where federal agencies overstep constitutional boundaries,” Ciccone said at the news conference.
Representative Leonela Felix, a Pawtucket Democrat, has joined Kallman in introducing a bill that would bar law enforcement from wearing masks or disguises when interacting with the public and require visible identification, with some exceptions.
“Across the country, people are seeing armed officers conducting operations while masked or unidentified,” Felix said. “That creates fear, confusion, and real danger for the public and for law enforcement officers alike.”
The measure would not prevent undercover operations or interfere with emergency responses, she said, but it would help protect residents and ensure accountability.
" Transparency is critical to public safety, and when people cannot identify law enforcement, the risk of impersonation rises,“ Felix said. ”Constitutional rights are in jeopardy, and trust between communities and law enforcement is eroded."
A similar bill has been proposed in Massachusetts and passed in California. But some law professors question whether states have the authority to enforce such laws.
Felix has also joined Senator Jonathon Acosta, a Central Falls Democrat, in backing legislation that would change the definition of a misdemeanor to be an offense with a maximum sentence of 364 days rather than 365 days.
While the difference is just one day, advocates say that can make a huge difference because federal immigration law allows undocumented immigrants, and even someone with a green card, to be detained or deported if convicted of an offense punishable by a sentence of a year or more.
The state Senate has passed similar legislation for each of the past five years, but it has not passed the House amid concerns raised by Attorney General Peter F. Neronha’s office.
“That is a great bill,” said Representative Karen Alzate, a Pawtucket Democrat and caucus cochair. “It feels like it’s low-hanging fruit because it can make a big impact.”
A bill introduced by Representative Arthur Handy, a Cranston Democrat, and Senator Melissa A. Murray, a Woonsocket Democrat, would remove the five-year waiting period to allow lawful permanent residents to receive benefits with delay through RI Works, the state’s primary cash assistance and economic support program for low-income families with children.
